children: U.S. automakers have been eager to consign AM radio to the history books. Instead, they have triggered the nearly unthinkable: a bipartisan push from Congress to save the century-old broadcast band.

An ensemble of advocates, including broadcasters and former federal emergency officials, have been pressing lawmakers for years to mandate AM radio after automakers such as Tesla, Volvo and BMW stopped providing those tuners in new models. Their push is working. On Tuesday, the House passed the AM Radio for Every Vehicle Act with overwhelming support.

The bill now heads to the Senate, where related legislation has 60 co-sponsors and bipartisan support. Supporters say the old-school technology remains a vital piece of the government's emergency communication network and that many Americans continue to depend on it.

"As much as our technology continues to evolve, nothing has changed that fact that if you don't have cell networks and you don't have power, radio is your lifeline," said Curtis LeGeyt, president and chief executive of the National Association of Broadcasters, an industry group.

At the same time, the bill presents an unexpected headache for the auto industry as it grapples with challenges including tariffs, higher fuel prices and the threat of upstart Chinese automakers from breaking into the U.S.
The industry's shift away from incorporating AM radio began a decade ago, after more car companies began to develop electric vehicles for the U.S. market.

Many carmakers have said that currents from EV motors can interfere with AM broadcast signals and have removed radio receivers from newer models as a result. An industry-funded study by the group Center for Automotive Research estimated it would cost automakers $3.8 billion to mitigate interference between EVs and AM radio.

Ford Motor was among the companies that initially dropped AM radio, but reversed course after Chief Executive Jim Farley said he spoke with policy leaders "about the importance of AM broadcast radio as a part of the emergency alert system." (A Ford spokesman didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.)

Yet carmakers have long been opposed to an AM radio mandate. Industry lobbyists have argued that AM radio is no longer a widely used feature and say that it can interfere with the widening suite of technology installed in new vehicles.
AM radio, which began more than 100 years ago and is used by more than 4,000 stations, has faded away as FM radio audiences grew over time.

Drivers nowadays have an array of options to get news, entertainment and emergency warnings, said John Bozzella, president and chief executive of the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, in comments in 2024 to lawmakers.
"Unlike lifesaving, and mandated, technologies like air bags, seat belts, electronic stability control and headlights, analog AM radio does not contribute to motor vehicle safety," Bozzella said.
If enacted, the Transportation Department would be required to issue a rule requiring AM radio within one year, and the authority to enforce the provision would expire after eight years.

"What makes this piece of legislation really stand out, and has shaped the advocacy around it, is the broad bipartisan support," LeGeyt said, "in a moment where Republicans and Democrats can't agree on just about anything."
